To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the rate of microbial activity in solid matrices declines with water content because of two mechanisms: (i) substrate diffusion limitation, and (ii) physiologic effects of cell dehydration.
both substrate supply and adverse physiological effects associated cell dehydration contribute to inhibition of microbial activity in soil at low water potentials.
both diffusional limitations and adverse physiological effects associated cell dehydration are important factors limiting microbial activity at low soil water potential.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of water on the activities of soil microorganisms.
the mechanisms by which water affects microbial activity.
the mechanisms by which soil water content influences microbial processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
substrate diffusion limitation and adverse physiological effects associated cell dehydration can explain the entire decline in microbial activity as soil water potential declines.

the relative importance of diffusional limitation and dehydration in controlling microbial activity depends on the specific soil system being studied and that it is necessary to evaluate both mechanisms in order to fully understand the effects of low water content on microbial activity in soil.
the relative importance of diffusional limitation and dehydration in controlling microbial activity in soil depends on both the water potential and the type of microbial activity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

diffusional limitations of substrate supply are the major factor limiting microbial activity at high water contents, and adverse physiological effects of cell dehydration are the major factor controlling microbial activity at lower water contents.
diffusional limitations and physiologic effects of cell dehydration are the major inhibiting factors controlling microbial activity in soils at water potentials below approximately 0.6MPa.

substrate supply and physiologic effects of cell dehydration both contribute to microbial inhibition in soils at low water content, but the relative importance of each varies with soil water potential.
The main takeaway from our work is that
diffusional limitations of substrate supply can be a major control on microbial activity in solid matrices, and that diffusional effects are likely to be more important than previously realized.
both substrate supply and physiological effects of low water content must be considered when evaluating the effects of water on microbial processes.
diffusional constraints and adverse physiological effects can explain the decline in microbial activity at low water contents.
